claims.claim: Vital signs are the basic measurements that reflect the body's essential functions; the OpenStax nursing textbooks describe them as markers of physiological homeostasis that are essential for monitoring a patient's progress.
The five vital signs measured in routine nursing care are temperature, pulse (heart rate), respirations (respiratory rate), blood pressure, and oxygen saturation (SpO2).

Adult reference ranges exist for each vital sign (roughly: temperature 97–99F by mouth, pulse 60–100, respirations 12–20, blood pressure below 120/80, oxygen saturation 95–100 percent), but the ranges vary by source and are only guides, because normal depends on age, sex, weight, exercise capability, and overall health.
What is normal for one person or one age group may be abnormal for another; vital sign parameters vary across the life span, so each patient's individual baseline must be considered.

Sudden changes in vital signs — such as a fever, an increased heart rate, or a drop in blood pressure — are signs that the body is out of balance, and monitoring them can help prevent a life-threatening emergency.

Vital signs are gathered at the first encounter to establish a baseline and routinely afterward; the combination of readings over time (the trend) defines what is normal for that individual patient, so a change from baseline matters even when the number is within the general range.

Nurses obtain, validate, interpret, and document vital signs and may recheck them at any time using nursing judgment; nursing assistants measure vital signs such as blood pressure and temperature as part of routine care and report changes to nurses.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Adult respiratory rate reference range: 12–18 breaths per minute (MedlinePlus) vs 12–20 breaths per minute (OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing).
positions: MedlinePlus medical encyclopedia lists breathing at 12 to 18 breaths per minute for the average healthy adult at rest.
OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing states the normal rate from adolescence through adulthood is 12 to 20 breaths per minute.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents respirations as roughly 12–20 per minute, attributed to the OpenStax nursing textbook (the subject's backbone), and keeps the framing deliberately approximate — 'roughly' — so the lesson does not assert false precision. The range difference between sources is also used to support the honest note that reference ranges vary by source.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Normal oral temperature range: MedlinePlus lists 97.7–99.1F (36.5–37.3C), while OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing Table 7.3 lists oral 96.4–99.1F (35.8–37.3C).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says 'roughly 97–99F (about 36–37C) by mouth,' which sits inside both ranges, and presents it as a guide rather than a precise cutoff. Both sources agree the average is about 98.6F (37C), which the lesson does not dispute.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether oxygen saturation is one of the 'vital signs': the classic list names four (temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure), while modern nursing practice measures oxygen saturation with the set.
positions: OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills defines vital signs as including temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, and blood pressure.

OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing explicitly names five vital signs including saturation of peripheral oxygen (SpO2), and the Clinical Nursing Skills vital-signs equipment list includes a pulse oximeter.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the five measurements used in routine practice — temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation — following the Fundamentals of Nursing text, and notes that each of the five has its own dedicated sibling lesson. This matches the curriculum's topic list, which includes oxygen-saturation as a sibling topic.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's claim that vital signs are 'a foundational concept in Nursing & Allied Health Foundations' with no clinical content was unsupported and was discarded as boilerplate.

The generated draft's vocabulary definitions ('Vital Signs — A foundational Nursing & Allied Health Foundations concept covered in this lesson') were circular and carried no information; all ten vocabulary definitions were replaced with independently sourced, non-circular definitions.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire machine-generated draft (definition-free boilerplate, toolbox-drawer analogy, circular vocabulary) with a clinically grounded lesson sourced to the OpenStax nursing textbooks, MedlinePlus, and BLS.
Attributed the working definition of vital signs to OpenStax and MedlinePlus rather than leaving it unattributed.
Stated the five vital signs (including oxygen saturation) explicitly, resolving the classic-four vs modern-five distinction with an attribution to the OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing text.
Kept adult reference ranges approximate and attributed (OpenStax + MedlinePlus), avoiding invented precision, and used the sources' range differences as the honest 'ranges vary' note.
All examples are original (Mei's post-surgery fever, Priya's clinical day, Mr. Kim's pulse, the check-engine-light analogy); none are taken from any source.
